newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - May 16.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- DILLONS BANKERS COLLECT MILLIONS

The announcement that SBC Warburg is to buy US investment bank Dillon Read will see all 52 partners at Dillon receive multi-million dollar payouts. However, the partners will not be able to cash in their payouts immediately after the estimated $600 million (375 million stg) deal is completed. Dutch bank ING Group, which had pulled out of talks with Dillon Read, will gain about $150 million through the sale to SBC of its 25 percent shareholding in the US bank.
-- MERCURY WARNING DESPITE 22 PERCENT LEAP

Fund management group Mercury Asset Management has warned shareholders that the strong rise in the world's stock markets is unsustainable. Commenting on the "phenomenal run" enjoyed by investors in equities recently, MAM vice chairman Carol Galley said "there is an element of destiny that we cannot control". The warning came as MAM reported a 22 percent leap in pre-tax profits to 171 million sterling for the year ending March.
-- BIRMINGHAM MIDSHIRES DOUBLES OPENING STAKE

Birmingham Midshires has moved to deter "carpetbaggers" from opening accounts in the expectation of a bank conversion or a take-over of the building society. The society raised the minimum opening balance for savings accounts from 1,000 stg to 2,500 stg. The move comes as new account openings were running at double what the society claims might be expected.
THE TIMES
-- GOVERNMENT TO CRACK DOWN ON LENDERS

The government has issued an unprecedented warning to lenders who charge vulnerable borrowers exorbitant rates of interest. Nigel Griffiths, Minister for Consumer Affairs, said that companies that specialise in lending to the poor had been put "under review". Companies under scrutiny could include Provident Financial and City Mortgage Corporation, both of whom extend loans to council tenants with bad credit ratings.
-- INFLATION FELL TO 2.5 PERCENT UNDER TORIES

Figures released Thursday from the Office of National Statistics show that the Conservative government achieved its long-promised target for inflation in April, before losing the general election on May 1. The figures show that the underlying rate of inflation fell to 2.5 percent in April. That total matches the target set by the Tory government to meet by the end of the last parliament.
-- CARPETBAGGERS CHALLENGE NATIONWIDE

Nationwide Building Society is facing a boardroom showdown over its mutual status next month when five campaigners in favour of a stock market floatation make a bid for election to the board. It is the first time that candidates in favour of conversion have succeeded in standing for election to a building society board.
THE GUARDIAN
-- AIRBUS SCORES OVER BOEING WITH 925 MILLION STG CHINA DEAL

Airbus Industrie, the European aerospace consortium, has secured a 925 million stg order from China for 30 aircraft. The order could create more than 12,000 jobs in Britain and across Europe, and has put Airbus on a par with arch-rival Boeing for orders in the world's fastest-growing aviation market.
-- EU ACCORD HELPS PART-TIMERS

A draft agreement between European Union employers and trade unions under the Maastricht Treaty's social protocol could see Britain's part-time workers win improved employment rights. The protocol, which was welcomed by the TUC, does not yet apply to the UK but the new Labour government has pledged to end Britain's opt-out at next month's EU summit in Amsterdam.
-- UTILITIES SHAKE-UP POSTPONED

Trade and Industry secretary Margaret Beckett is understood to have moved reform of utilities regulation to a low priority, lest the Labour government damage its new rapport with business. The shift of emphasis could see a postponement of the pre- election pledge to shake-up utilities regulation, and a concentration instead on preparing the country for the onset of competition in gas and electricity next year.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- ARNAULT'S NO SHOW STIRS SHAREHOLDERS AT GUINNESS AGM

Tony Greener, chairman of Guinness, has denied there is a "rift" between him and Bernard Arnault, the only Guinness board member to oppose the planned merger with Grand Metropolitan. The issue was raised when an ordinary shareholder at the group's annual general meeting questioned the absence of Arnault from the podium. Greener told the meeting that Arnault was attending another board meeting and had sent his apologies.
-- REGIONAL PAPER IN BID TALKS

Regional newspaper publisher Adscene is reported to be in "serious talks" with a potential bidder. According to industry sources, Harry Lambert, the group's chairman and chief executive, is understood to have received approaches from several regional newspaper groups and has held formal talks with one of them. Any takeover would confirm the trend towards rationalisation of the regional newspaper market.
-- MIDLAND TO CREATE 600 PHONE BANKING JOBS

Midland Bank is to open a fourth telephone banking centre, creating up to 600 jobs in Scotland. The bank said the new centre was necessary to help cope with increasing customer demand. Midland also announced plans to extend its telephone service to take calls seven days a week.
